title: Site a relay beacon with sight of habitat and rover
instruction: Stand the white relay beacon upright on the grey plateau where it has a clear straight line of sight from its centre to the centre of the blue habitat and to the centre of the orange rover. The dark ridges block sight.
context: Radio links on the lunar surface need direct line of sight, and at the planned south pole sites crater rims and ridges block it, so relay masts are sited on ground that sees both a habitat and a work site. This tabletop terrain model keeps that rule. Three dark ridges, taller than everything else, stand on a plateau with a habitat and a rover, and the beacon must stand where the straight line from its centre to the centre of each site clears every ridge. About 13 percent of the free plateau qualifies, in one pocket. A blind upright placement on the free plateau averages about 0.24. The plateau centre and the midpoint between the sites earn 0.25, each seeing only the rover, and the plateau edge nearest the start earns 0, so centring, symmetry or convenience never reach 1.0. The test is visibility reasoning about occluders; the motor part is one pick and place. A 1 g bench model; nothing about lunar gravity or radio propagation is claimed.
setup: On the table in front of the left arm (x forward from the arm bases, y left). Positions are table coordinates in metres, origin on the base line at the midline; the left arm's base is at (0, 0.305) and heights are above the table top. Every part is a rigid matte primitive with one friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Fixed: the plateau, a grey (sRGB 0.60, 0.60, 0.62) slab 220 mm along x, 270 mm along y and 12 mm tall, centred at (0.240, 0.255), spanning x 0.130 to 0.350 and y 0.120 to 0.390. Standing on the plateau, all fixed: the habitat, a light blue (sRGB 0.45, 0.65, 0.90) box 40 x 40 x 40 mm centred at (0.325, 0.365), top 52 mm up; the rover, an orange (sRGB 0.95, 0.55, 0.10) box 40 x 40 x 30 mm centred at (0.325, 0.145), top 42 mm up; three ridges, charcoal (sRGB 0.18, 0.18, 0.18) boxes 80 mm long, 12 mm thick and 70 mm tall, tops 82 mm up. Ridge 1 is centred at (0.268, 0.177), its long axis 120 degrees from +x, its centreline running from (0.248, 0.212) to (0.288, 0.142). Ridge 2 is centred at (0.308, 0.295), its long axis along x, from x 0.268 to 0.348. Ridge 3 is centred at (0.197, 0.296), its long axis 135 degrees from +x, its centreline running from (0.169, 0.324) to (0.225, 0.268). Loose: the beacon, a white (sRGB 0.95, 0.95, 0.95) cylinder 30 mm in diameter and 45 mm tall, 40 g, standing upright on the table at (0.170, 0.075), its edge 30 mm from the plateau's inboard edge (y = 0.120). On the plateau its top is 57 mm up, so every ridge top is at least 25 mm above the beacon, the habitat and the rover. On a 5 mm grid of beacon centres that stand clear of every ridge and site (about 41,700 square mm), about 5,600 square mm (13 percent) have clear lines from the beacon's centre to both site centres, nearly all in one pocket spanning x 0.155 to 0.250 and y 0.285 to 0.390; 41 percent see exactly one site and 45 percent see neither. The demo's spot, (0.205, 0.365), is 48 mm from ridge 3. The right arm is idle at its ready pose. To build it: a 12 mm board for the plateau, painted grey and taped to the table; three 80 x 12 x 70 mm wood blocks painted charcoal and glued on edge at the stated centres and angles; two painted wood blocks for the habitat and the rover, each with the centre of its top marked; the beacon from a 30 mm white acrylic or acetal rod cut to 45 mm (about 40 g), or a wooden dowel weighted to 40 g; tape a mark for its start.
scoring: End state only, judged after the arm withdraws, with a tape measure and a thread; a photo records the end state. The beacon stands on the plateau when it is upright (axis within 5 degrees of vertical, either end up), at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s), its lowest point within 4 mm of the plateau top and its centre inside the plateau's 220 x 270 mm outline. A link runs from the beacon's centre to a site's centre. For each site, stretch a thread from the centre of the beacon's top to the marked centre of the site's top; the link is clear when the thread passes at least 4 mm, measured horizontally, from every ridge's footprint. Equivalently, measure the beacon's centre with the tape and test the straight segment from it to the site's centre against each ridge's footprint in plan. The thread runs 42 to 57 mm up, below every 82 mm ridge top, so the plan view of the footprints decides. Do not draw the lines on a perspective photo: in the oblique top view a ridge's top appears 40 to 50 mm beyond its footprint, which changes the verdict, at the demo's spot among others. Score 1.0: standing on the plateau with both links clear, the success condition, which ends the trial once it has held for 1 s. Score 0.25: standing on the plateau with exactly one link clear. Score 0: standing on the plateau with neither link clear, and every beacon that does not stand on the plateau: on the table, lying down, tilted more than 5 degrees, still moving, held above the plateau, on a ridge, the habitat or the rover, or with its centre outside the outline. Every outcome falls in exactly one tier. Reference outcomes: the start state 0, the beacon is on the table; the plateau centre (0.240, 0.255) and the midpoint between the sites (0.325, 0.255) 0.25, each sees only the rover; beside the habitat at (0.280, 0.370) 0.25, it sees only the habitat; the plateau spot nearest the start, (0.170, 0.140), 0, it sees neither; the demo's spot (0.205, 0.365) 1.0, its lines clear the ridges by 48 and 19 mm. Sliding or knocking cannot score: the beacon starts on the table, 12 mm below the plateau top, and counts only once it stands on the plateau; a knocked beacon lies down. A value exactly on a limit passes, with a 0.1 mm margin on lengths. In simulation the tests use the beacon's centre and quaternion: the lowest point comes from the centre and the axis, and a link is the exact distance between the horizontal segment joining the two centres and each ridge's rectangular footprint, 0 when they cross. The plateau, ridges and sites are fixed in simulation; on the real rig a trial in which any of them moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0. The scorer reads object poses, not the gripper: in simulation a beacon held motionless in a scoring place would count; on real arms the end state is judged after the arm parks.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand the beacon upright back on its mark on the table; the plateau, the ridges, the habitat and the rover do not move. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the open-loop demo is built from the nominal start.
fidelity: Approximate: the terrain is flat blocks, not slopes, and every ridge is taller than every object, so line of sight reduces to a straight line between centres in plan view. Radio effects (Fresnel zone, diffraction, antenna height) are not modelled; the 4 mm margin stands in for them. The beacon is a rigid cylinder, not a mast. One shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), matte colours; the fixtures cannot move. Earth gravity on a bench.
